claims.text: High-temperature oxidation resistance and material integrity in MPEAs are governed primarily by the formation and stability of protective oxide scales.
Protective-scale formation depends on the presence and distribution of oxygen-affine elements such as Al, Cr, or Si.
Al, Cr, and Si can form continuous, adherent oxide layers in MPEAs.
Local surface composition and microstructural homogeneity influence oxide-scale formation kinetics and morphology.
Systematically changing Al, Cr, or Si concentration while holding other elements and processing constant provides a controlled comparison of protective-element effects.
Continuous, adherent Al2O3, Cr2O3, or SiO2 surface scales are the proposed structural mediator.
Elements with high oxygen affinity segregate to the alloy surface.
Surface-enriched oxygen-affine elements form protective oxide scales.
Protective oxide scales act as diffusion barriers that retard further oxidation.
Scale continuity, adherence, and resistance to spallation determine protective effectiveness.
Surface composition and microstructure influence scale continuity, adherence, and spallation resistance.
MPEAs containing sufficient Al, Cr, or Si will have lower mass gain per unit area than baseline alloys lacking sufficient concentrations of these elements.
MPEAs containing sufficient Al, Cr, or Si will form more stable and adherent oxide scales than the baseline alloys.
MPEAs containing sufficient Al, Cr, or Si will retain mechanical integrity better after oxidation exposure than the baseline alloys.
The proposed governing behavior should hold above 1000°C when the surface is homogeneous and has not been depleted of protective elements.
